bedroom:
Somewhere to sleep that isn't the floor of the hall. A bedroom holds the household's beds, chests and a hearth, and every Bastion needs a few before anyone wants to stay the winter.

Bedrooms add beds, so more people can live at the Bastion without crowding, and they become one of the owners' basic facilities. A larger bedroom holds more beds and can be enlarged later.
dining-room:
A long table, a good fire and the whole household eating together. Shared meals are where the Bastion's people stop being strangers.

A dining room raises Comfort. It is a basic facility, and it can be enlarged as the household grows.
parlor:
A quiet, well-furnished room for receiving guests of standing: envoys, merchants with a proposal, a lord passing through.

The parlor lifts Comfort and the Bastion's standing with visitors. A Bastion has only one; enlarge it instead of building another.
courtyard:
Open ground inside the walls: where carts unload, children play, the well stands and the garrison musters.

A courtyard is a basic facility and makes room for things that need space. A roomy courtyard or larger is where a Training Yard can be laid out. A Bastion has only one.
kitchen:
The heart of any household: a great hearth, ovens, copper pots and a cook who rules it all.

A kitchen feeds the people who live at the Bastion and is needed before an Inn or a Great Hall can be built. It is a basic facility and can be enlarged.
storage:
Vaulted rooms of sacks, crates, barrels and casks, counted by lantern light.

Storage raises how much food and goods the Bastion can keep, which matters most when a siege closes the roads. It is a basic facility and can be enlarged.
wall:
A ring around the grounds, begun as a timber palisade and raised over the years: a stone wall, reinforced with buttresses, and finally a wall walk with crenellations where defenders fight under cover.

The wall multiplies the garrison's strength and gives the Bastion Integrity that an attacker has to wear down before breaking in. Each step up is priced along the whole length of the wall; extending the grounds lengthens it. A Bastion has one wall.
spike-barricade:
Rows of sharpened stakes at the foot of the wall, angled outward, between the wall and any ditch or moat.

The barricade adds a little to the defense and blunts light siege engines. It is built once and grows with the wall when the grounds are extended.
gatehouse:
The gate is the weakest part of any wall, so it gets towers of its own: a fortified gate passage with rooms above for the guards.

A gatehouse adds Integrity and makes the walls harder to take. It is the base for the Barbican, Portcullis and Drawbridge.
barbican:
An outer gate in front of the gatehouse, so attackers who break through the first gate find themselves in a killing ground before the second.

The barbican strengthens the defense of a walled Bastion with a gatehouse.
portcullis:
Iron grilles that drop in the gate passage, and holes in the vault above for pouring down whatever is at hand.

A portcullis with murder holes makes the gate far costlier to force and adds to the defense.
drawbridge:
A bridge that lifts on chains, leaving a gap a ram can't cross.

Battering rams can't reach the gate, so light engines do less damage to the wall. It needs a ditch or moat to span.
arrow-slits:
Narrow slits in the stone and timber galleries hung out over the wall, so archers can shoot straight down at anyone at the foot of it.

Defenders fight from cover, adding to the defense of a walled Bastion.
watchtower:
A tall tower with a lookout who sees trouble on the horizon long before it arrives.

Each watchtower adds to the defense, up to a limit. The first one stands at the heart of the grounds; more go on the corners of the wall. Several can be built.
dry-ditch:
A deep, steep-sided ditch dug around the walls: attackers have to climb down and up again under fire.

The ditch adds to the defense and keeps siege engines and ladders back from the wall.
wet-moat:
Water all round the walls, wide and still.

A moat multiplies the defense and halves the damage of light siege engines, and nobody digs under a wall through water.
ballista:
A great crossbow on a stone platform, with a crew to wind it and bolts as long as a man.

Each emplacement cuts the damage siege engines do and adds its crew to the garrison. Several can be built.
postern:
A small hidden door at the foot of the wall and a tunnel beyond it, known to few.

During a siege, food and messengers slip in and out: the stores last longer and envoys get through the lines.
lesser-wards:
Glyphs cut into the gate and walls, alarms that ring when something crosses them, and charms against fire.

Lesser wards cut the damage magic does in a siege.
greater-wards:
A shimmering dome of protection anchored by runes on every tower.

Greater wards cut magical damage further, and nobody scries into the Bastion or teleports in or out. They build on the lesser wards.
granary:
A tall timber store raised on stones to keep the grain dry and the rats out.

The granary raises how much food the Bastion can store for lean years and sieges. It counts as a basic storage facility on the owners' sheets.
well:
A stone well inside the walls: water whenever it's wanted.

With a well, the Bastion never runs out of water, siege or not.
deep-well:
A shaft bored down through bedrock where an ordinary well finds nothing, with a treadwheel to haul the water up.

Like a well, it gives the Bastion unlimited water, on ground where a well can't be dug.
cistern:
A vaulted underground tank that catches the rain and holds it.

The cistern stores water for a siege when there is no well: a set number of days' water for everyone inside.
smokehouse:
Hams and fish hanging in the smoke, barrels of salt, meat packed for the winter.

Food keeps longer, so the Bastion's stores hold more.
kitchen-garden:
Neat beds of cabbages, beans and herbs inside the walls.

The garden grows food every day, and because it's inside the walls it keeps growing during a siege. Walled and terraced, it grows more.
orchard:
Rows of apple and pear trees beside the Bastion.

The orchard grows food every day and sells its surplus for a little income each turn.

Planted out into groves and then a cider estate, it feeds more people and sells more fruit.
fields:
Patchwork fields worked by tenant farmers who pay rent in grain and coin.

Fields grow food and pay rent; how much depends on the land and the climate. They can be upgraded to estate farms and a great estate.
livestock:
Pens of sheep, pigs, goats and cattle beside the barn.

Livestock adds food every day and animals to sell.

A dairy and piggery, and later a whole cattle ranch, raise bigger herds: more food and more to sell.
mill:
A watermill on the stream, grinding the Bastion's grain and its neighbours'.

The mill raises what the fields produce and earns a little each turn.
hunting-lodge:
A rustic lodge at the forest's edge, antlers on the gable, hounds in the yard.

Hunting brings in food every day, the hides and furs are sold for a little gold each turn, and the lodge's hunts add to the Bastion's Renown.
workers-lodge:
A sturdy hall for the builders who stay on year-round.

The lodge houses a permanent building crew: one more crew working on projects, with no upkeep to pay.
clear-trail:
A narrow way cut through forest and hill to the nearest settlement.

A trail along the whole route makes the Bastion easier to reach: travel is faster, merchants come more often and income from visitors grows. Built per mile.
build-road:
A proper road with a gravel bed and ditches, wide enough for carts.

A road along the whole route improves Accessibility further. It follows a cleared trail.
pave-road:
A paved highway: stone laid on a deep bed, built to last centuries.

The best road there is: the highest Accessibility a road can give. Once the road is paved, there is nothing more to build on it.
timber-bridge:
A sturdy timber bridge over the river on the road to the Bastion.

The bridge raises Accessibility.
stone-bridge:
An arched stone bridge that floods and years won't take.

It raises Accessibility further than a timber bridge.
pier:
A timber pier where boats can tie up and unload.

Boats can land at the Bastion, which raises Accessibility.
harbor:
Quays, cranes and warehouses for sea or river trade.

A harbor draws exotic traders and earns income that grows with Accessibility. It can be upgraded to a trading port.
waystation:
A roadside station with stables and fresh horses.

Relay riders change horses here: Accessibility rises, and with a Coach House envoys ride even faster.
coach-house:
A carriage house and stables of fresh remounts kept ready.

Envoys ride far faster carrying the party's orders home, faster still with a Waystation.
hidden-approach:
An overgrown way through trees and rocks, so the Bastion is hard to find from the road.

Concealment rises a lot, but the Bastion is a little harder for friends to reach too.
market-square:
Stalls, a fountain and a market day that draws the countryside in.

The market earns fees and rent each turn and draws merchants. It grows into a market hall and then a market town.
inn:
A warm inn by the road, ale by the fire and travellers with news.

Travellers pay for beds and drink each turn and bring a rumor with them. It needs a kitchen, and grows into a coaching inn and a grand hostelry.
brewery:
Copper kettles, oak barrels and the smell of malt.

The brewery earns a little each turn and makes an Inn far more profitable. It can be expanded up to ten times: each expansion costs more than the last and brews a little more, but needs more brewers, who need beds, food and wages. From the second expansion on it brews more than its brewers cost.
craftsmens-row:
A lane of workshops let to smiths, carpenters and weavers.

The workshops pay rent, and crafted goods sell for more. It grows into a guild street and an artisans' quarter.
warehouse:
A large store stacked high with bales and barrels, and a clerk who knows where everything is.

Visiting merchants bring more stock.
merchant-charter:
A sealed charter that tells the trading houses the Bastion is open for business.

Better merchants come: the merchant tier rises by one.

The charter can be extended up to ten times: each extension brings more traders and more fees, and more clerks to house, feed and pay. From the second extension on the fees cover the clerks.
tollgate:
A barrier on the road and a keeper taking coin from every cart.

Tolls earn income that grows with Accessibility.
lumber-camp:
Felled logs, a sawpit and woodcutters at the forest's edge.

Timber projects cost less, and once upgraded to a sawmill it sells planks. Whenever no timber project is under way, the camp sells what it fells instead, and earns twice as much.
quarry:
Workers cutting stone blocks from the hillside, a crane lifting them out.

Stone projects cost less. Whenever no stone project is under way, the quarry sells what it cuts instead, and earns twice as much.

The quarry can be opened up to ten levels: each costs more than the last and cuts a little more stone, with more quarrymen to house, feed and pay. Once it is stoneworks it earns more than its quarrymen cost.
mine:
Timbered tunnels into the hill, ore carts and miners' lanterns.

A mine earns big income with some risk; gems pay double. It grows into a deep mine and a mining company.

Past the mining company the shafts can go deeper still, up to ten levels: each costs more than the last and digs out a little more, with more miners to house, feed and pay.
trading-company:
The Bastion's own caravans under its own banner.

The late-game income that pays the party: it grows into a regional trading house and a merchant princedom.
strongroom:
A vaulted room behind an iron-bound door, with chests counted twice.

The treasury is safe from theft, and letters of credit let the party pay for things far from home.
servants-quarters:
Simple, tidy rooms for the people who keep the Bastion running.

The quarters add beds and let the Bastion hire servants. They count as a basic bedroom on the owners' sheets.
bathhouse:
A steamy room with a warm pool and tiled walls.

Comfort rises, and a long rest here takes away an extra level of exhaustion.
chapel:
A small chapel within the walls, light falling through coloured glass.

Comfort and Renown rise, and the defenders take heart.
infirmary:
Cots, bandages, herbs and a healer.

After an attack, half the defenders who would have died survive wounded.
training-yard:
Targets, dummies and sparring rings where the garrison drills every day.

Defenders count for more. It needs a roomy courtyard.
garrison-hall:
Barracks, an armoury rack and long tables for the guards.

The hall lets the Bastion hire guards, who are paid each turn.

Built up into barracks, a barracks ward and finally a citadel garrison, it houses up to a hundred hired guards for the largest keeps.
great-hall:
Banners, a high table and room for a feast.

Renown rises, and the owners can hold feasts. It needs a kitchen.
guest-wing:
Fine rooms set apart for visitors.

Guests and refugees have somewhere to stay, and paying visitors pay more.
stewards-office:
Ledgers, maps and a steward who writes everything down.

Standing orders run while the owners are away, and the steward sends a report every turn.
pleasure-gardens:
Hedges, fountains and marble statues for strolling and being seen.

Comfort and Renown rise.
rookery:
A tower of roosting messenger birds and a keeper who knows each one.

Birds carry the party's orders home, for a small cost each.
beacon-tower:
A tall tower with a great fire laid ready on top.

Preset signals reach the Bastion at once, and the watch adds to Security. A Bastion has one beacon.
sending-station:
A quiet chamber where a pair of sending stones rests on a pedestal.

Once a day an order goes home and a reply comes back at once. It needs a pair of sending stones.
scrying-pool:
A still, dark pool that shows what the seer asks to see.

Once a day the owners can see the Bastion as it is, wherever they are.
arcane-lanterns:
Lanterns that float along the battlements and never go out.

Security rises, and night attacks lose their surprise.
fishery:
Boats drawn up on the bank, nets drying on poles and a smoke shed full of the day's catch.

A fishery on a stream, river, lake or the sea feeds the Bastion every day and sells the surplus. Weirs and traps, and later a fishing fleet, bring in more. It needs open water: it stops during a siege.
greenhouse:
Rows of small glass panes in an iron frame, warmed by braziers through the winter.

A greenhouse grows vegetables and herbs inside the walls all year, so its food keeps coming during a siege. Expanded into glass gardens and an orangery, it grows more and brightens the household's days.
trading-post:
A counting house with a loading yard: clerks with ledgers, carters, and a wall map of every road the Bastion trades along.

No trade route can be made until the Bastion has a Trading Post. Each one handles three routes and earns a little in fees, and a Bastion can build several, so the number of routes it keeps grows with them. Its clerks and carters live at the Bastion: they need beds and food, and draw wages.
hunters-guild:
A timber guildhall hung with antlers and furs, its yard busy with hounds, pack ponies and drying racks.

The guild's hunters and trappers range far beyond the walls, so it feeds the Bastion even where there is little game close by and nothing grows, and their pelts bring in gold every turn. Upgraded into a trappers' and rangers' lodge and then a great hunt, it brings in much more meat and fur money, and makes the Bastion's name known. The hunters live at the Bastion and need beds, food and wages, which the pelts pay for once the guild is a great hunt; the hunt stops during a siege.
highland-herds:
Goats and hardy sheep picking their way over the scree, with dry-stone folds and a shepherd's hut on the slope.

Herds on the hills, mountains or barren land give milk, cheese, wool and meat where no field would grow. Summer pastures and a drovers' station keep bigger flocks. The herds are outside the walls: they stop feeding the Bastion during a siege.
mushroom-cellars:
Vaulted cellars under the keep, with racks of straw and logs pale with mushrooms.

The cellars grow food inside the walls anywhere at all, even underground, and keep growing through a siege. They take no room on the grounds. Deeper cellars and fungus caverns grow more.
